body:
SEO brief template for writers: completed template. A well-written SEO brief shortens the journey from commission to published article, because the writer knows in advance which keyword to target, what structure the editor expects and which pages the text should link to.

Without a written brief, the editor often receives a grammatically correct text on a different subject from the one commissioned. The template below can be copied directly into a document or an online form.

SEO brief template for writers: completed template

A brief is not a summary of the article, but a set of clear constraints that the writer follows while writing. The more precise the constraints, the fewer corrections are needed later.

The template below has nine fields, each filled in with a real example for a hypothetical corporate blog article. You can adapt it directly to your own subject, keeping the same field order.

Why a written brief beats verbal instructions

A phone conversation or a short message leaves room for interpretation. The writer remembers what they understood, not necessarily what the editor meant to communicate.

The difference between the two only becomes apparent once the text is ready, when corrections already cost time. A written brief eliminates this game of telephone, because the writer can refer back to it while writing.

The editor, in turn, checks the result against a specific document, rather than a memory of the conversation. The advantage is particularly clear when you work with several external contributors, rather than just one person.

Without a common format, each article ends up structured differently, and consistency is only addressed during editing. A written brief also helps onboard a new writer, who learns the site's conventions from completed examples rather than from memory.

What a complete SEO brief contains

A complete brief answers four questions before the writer writes the first word: what the reader is looking for, how the text is organized, which pages it links to and who it is for.

The keyword and search intent

The keyword is the phrase the reader searches for in Google, and search intent is the reason behind the search. For "SEO brief", the intent is informational: someone wants a ready-to-use template, not just a definition.

The brief specifies both, plus a few closely related variations that the text can cover naturally. If you do not know which variations to include, start with the keyword generator, available free on the site.

The required article structure

The structure sets out how many H2 sections the article has, what each contains and whether lists or a specific example are needed, such as a table or a completed template. Without this part, the writer improvises their own structure, which rarely fits the rest of the blog.

For writers who also handle the actual wording of sentences, the guide on how to write a page that answers adds further detail to this field of the brief.

Required internal links

Each brief specifies at least two service or tool pages that the article must link to, plus a few published articles on related subjects. The writer does not invent URLs, but chooses from a list provided by the editor.

For example, an article about building backlinks almost always links to the link buildingpage. The same logic applies to any other service page relevant to the subject covered.

Tone, audience and what to avoid

The final part describes who the text is for and what is prohibited: invented figures, unrealistic promises or comparisons naming competitors. This section prevents the most expensive corrections, those related to content rather than form.

For example, a brief for this blog explicitly specifies the formal form of "you" and prohibits comparing the agency with other companies in the field by name. Without this written instruction, a new writer tends to reproduce the more informal tone seen on other sites.

Who fills in the brief and how much time to allow

The brief is usually filled in by the person who knows the content strategy best: an SEO specialist, an editor or the business owner when the team is small. The writer receives a finished brief and does not participate in filling it in.

For a typical blog article, filling in a brief using the template below takes between ten and fifteen minutes if the person already has the keyword list and internal links available. It only takes longer when the subject is new and requires a preliminary check for duplicate content.

This preliminary check is the step most often skipped, especially under the pressure of a strict editorial calendar. A brief sent without it risks commissioning an article on a subject already covered, causing the two texts to cannibalize each other in Google.

The completed template, field by field

Below is a completed brief for a hypothetical article about choosing a hosting provider. Copy the structure and replace the values with those for your own subject.

  • Proposed title: How to choose a hosting provider for an online store.
  • Keyword: hosting provider for an online store.
  • Search intent: informational; the reader is comparing options before buying.
  • Target audience: owners of small online stores without advanced technical knowledge.
  • Required structure: a two-paragraph introduction, followed by five H2 sections, including one with a table of criteria and one with a list of questions to ask the provider.
  • Target length: 1700 words, with a range between 1500 and 2000.
  • Required internal links: the recommended hosting services page and a published article about migrating a site without losing traffic.
  • Tone: explanatory, using the formal form of "you", with no unexplained technical terms.
  • What to avoid: direct criticism of competing providers by name, and performance figures without a verifiable source.

For the title field, take inspiration from the SEO title examples previously published on the blog. For the summary that appears below the title in Google, use the same reasoning as in the meta description examples.

Second example: a brief for an article with examples

Articles in the "Examples of..." or "Template for..." format need a slightly different brief, because the core of the text is the examples themselves, rather than explanations about them. Below is a completed brief for this format.

  • Proposed title: Return policy examples for an online store: 15 templates by product category.
  • Keyword: return policy examples.
  • Search intent: informational; the reader is looking for text ready to adapt, not theory about returns.
  • Required structure: a short introduction, followed by the 15 numbered examples in separate blocks, each with a one-sentence explanation of when to use it.
  • Mandatory rule: each example is a complete text that the reader can copy directly, not just an example title.
  • Required internal links: the ecommerce services page and a published article about an online store's terms and conditions.

The main difference from the first example is the mandatory rule about complete text. Without it, a rushed writer writes only example titles, without the actual content, and the article no longer solves anything for the reader.

A brief with these fields filled in can be written in a few minutes. It resolves most misunderstandings that would otherwise only emerge after the article is delivered.

The brief for updating an existing article

Updating an old article requires a shorter brief, but with an extra field compared with those above: what has changed since publication and what remains valid. Without this field, the writer rewrites the entire article, even though only a few paragraphs may have been outdated.

The internal links field is checked again at every update, because some URLs used originally may no longer exist or may have been redirected in the meantime. The same check is made for figures or prices mentioned in the text, which become outdated faster than the rest of the content.

A good update brief explicitly states whether the publication date stays as originally set or changes, because the answer influences how the reader interprets the age of the information. This decision is not left to the writer.

On a blog that has been inactive for a few months following a pause in the editorial calendar, updating older articles is often just as useful as publishing new ones. A written update brief saves exactly the same time as one for an article started from scratch.

How to check whether the brief is ready to send

Before sending the brief to the writer, run through a few quick checks. They eliminate the most common reasons for sending work back.

  • The keyword appears once, exactly as it should be used, not as a list of variations.
  • The structure has at least five H2 sections, with a clear idea for each.
  • The specified internal links actually exist and are published, not scheduled or imagined.
  • The audience and tone are described specifically, not using general words such as "professional".
  • The target length is given in words, not phrased vaguely as "as much as needed".

If one of these points is missing, the writer fills the gap with their own interpretation. The result almost certainly differs from what you had in mind when you commissioned it.

Common mistakes that make briefs useless

A long brief is not automatically a good brief. A few mistakes occur frequently and cancel out the document's entire advantage.

  • The keyword is chosen off the top of your head, without checking whether the subject is already covered by an existing article.
  • The structure asks for "the same sections as article X", without actually listing those sections.
  • Internal links are described vaguely, such as "relevant links", without specific URLs attached.
  • The brief asks for a particular tone, but the examples previously sent to the writer have different tones from one another.
  • The length is not mentioned at all, and the article ends up either too short or padded with sentences lacking substance.

Each of these mistakes can be fixed by explicitly filling in the missing field. Explanations sent later in chat, after the writer has already written the text, always arrive too late.

A complete SEO brief turns writing from an exchange of unclear messages into a repeatable process. The template above works equally well for a blog article and for texts supporting SEO optimization or technical SEOpages.
